analysis.one_liner: Strips legal liability protection from social media companies and bans them from deplatforming U.S. citizens for their views.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. George Santos with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on April 17, 2023, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Section 230 of the Communications Act, the legal shield that generally keeps platforms from being sued over content their users post. It would remove that protection for social media companies and make it illegal for them to suspend, restrict, or reduce engagement with a U.S. citizen's account because of the citizen's social, political, or religious status — even if the citizen clearly violated the platform's rules on hate speech, harassment, discrimination, or violent threats. Companies that deplatform a citizen would owe a $5,000 civil penalty for each day of the restriction. The bill was introduced by Rep. George Santos with no cosponsors and was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat with no further action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be users (most prominently, politically active figures) who feel they were wrongly banned, throttled, or deplatformed by Facebook, Twitter/X, Instagram, or TikTok. They would gain a federal right to keep their accounts active regardless of policy violations, with a $5,000-a-day penalty against companies that restrict them. Internet users generally would gain a new way to sue platforms over user-posted content, since the bill removes Section 230 protection from social media services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users banned or throttled by major platforms

how_it_helps.text: For users who feel unfairly banned or throttled by a major platform, the bill would create a federal cause of action: a $5,000-a-day penalty for each day a platform restricts a U.S. citizen's account over their social, political, or religious views, even for clear policy violations.

It would strip Section 230 liability protection from social media companies, meaning they could be sued over content their users post — a change some advocates argue would make platforms more accountable for what they amplify.

analysis.who_pays: Social media companies would bear the costs: civil penalties of $5,000 per day of deplatforming, exposure to lawsuits over user content they could no longer moderate freely, and the loss of the Section 230 shield. Users of those platforms would also pay indirectly — platforms forced to host rule-violating content on any topic would likely become more hostile and less moderated, and the end of liability protection could lead platforms to delete far more content preemptively.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media companies and their users

drawbacks.text: The bill would require platforms to host users even when they clearly violate policies against hate speech, harassment, discrimination, or violent threats, backed by civil penalties — which its critics would say forces private companies to amplify abusive and dangerous speech.

Removing Section 230 liability protection for social media providers would expose them to lawsuits over user-posted content, likely pushing platforms to delete vast amounts of lawful speech and could financially strain smaller services.

The bill appears drafted around specific named companies (Meta, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, TikTok), raising questions about how it would apply as platforms change, and it never received a hearing or analysis of its feasibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real underlying grievance: a handful of platforms control much of public speech and users have little recourse when deplatformed. But this bill's remedy is badly designed — it would strip liability protection that shields the entire internet ecosystem, force platforms to host hate speech and threats by law, and channel $5,000-a-day fines to government rather than any relief to users. Its death in committee cost ordinary people essentially nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. George Santos introduced the bill on April 17, 2023, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no subcommittee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress.
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill.
Santos' own House tenure was cut short: he was expelled from the House in December 2023, removing any realistic path for the bill's sponsor to push it forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media companies and other online services that benefit from Section 230 liability protection are better off, since the threat to their shield never advanced. Deplatformed users gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social media companies; the bill never advanced

for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

against.name: House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill on the floor before the 118th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no party-level position on it was ever visible in the record.

industries.industry: Social media platforms (Meta, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, TikTok)
industries.note: The bill names specific companies and would strip their Section 230 liability shield and bar most deplatforming, with $5,000-a-day penalties for violations. Had it passed, it would have forced them to host violating content and exposed them to lawsuits over user posts.

industries.industry: Internet services and websites relying on Section 230 more broadly
industries.note: The bill amends Section 230 for 'social media services' as broadly defined, so some services beyond the named platforms could lose liability protection, raising litigation risk. Others would be unaffected.
